strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: improving visual grounding efficiency for deployable VLMs rather than only scaling model size. The motivation is well aligned with ECCV interests in efficient vision-language systems.

The empirical results are strong on the reported benchmarks. EGM consistently improves multiple QwenVL and InternVL model sizes on RefCOCO/+/g, with especially large gains for smaller Qwen models and competitive or better accuracy than much larger models at lower reported GPU latency.

The paper identifies a plausible failure mode for small grounding VLMs, namely linguistically complex referring expressions with multiple similar candidates, and uses this analysis to motivate concise reasoning traces.

The extension to amodal grounding is interesting and potentially valuable. Curating text prompts for COCO-Amodal/TAO-Amodal and evaluating VLM amodal localization opens a useful direction beyond standard RefCOCO grounding.

The method is described with enough implementation detail to understand the training recipe: SFT reasoning data generation, learnability-based RL data selection, GRPO-style optimization, reward definition, prompts, hyperparameters, and inference settings are mostly provided.
weaknesses: The central framing as test-time scaling is somewhat overstated. The gains come from substantial supervised fine-tuning and RL using generated reasoning traces, not simply from allocating more inference tokens to an existing small model. This weakens the conceptual novelty relative to reasoning distillation plus task-specific RL.

The experimental evidence lacks key ablations. It is unclear how much improvement comes from SFT alone, RL alone, learnability-based sampling, concise reasoning traces, additional task-specific training data, or simply fine-tuning without reasoning. Without these controls, the mechanism behind the gains is not convincingly isolated.

The amodal benchmark construction and evaluation rely heavily on proprietary VLM-generated prompts and verification, with no reported human validation of prompt correctness, uniqueness, or benchmark noise. This makes the amodal results promising but not yet fully reliable as evidence for general amodal grounding ability.

The failure-mode analysis is partly circular and subjective: GPT-4 is given model predictions and ground truth boxes and asked to categorize failures, and the paper then uses this to support the proposed reasoning approach. More quantitative linguistic-complexity analysis or human annotation would strengthen the claim.

Generality is still limited. Standard grounding evaluation is almost entirely on RefCOCO-family splits, while the training data are derived from RefCOCO-style data; there is little evidence of transfer to substantially different grounding datasets, open-vocabulary referring expressions, detection-style benchmarks, robotics/autonomous-driving data, or real deployment settings.

The paper compares against very large baseline models, but does not compare to strong task-specific distillation, LoRA fine-tuning without chain-of-thought, self-training, or other efficient grounding adaptation baselines. This leaves uncertainty about whether EGM is the best or most novel way to obtain the reported efficiency gains.

Reproducibility is a concern: the manuscript says code/website are coming soon, and the data curation depends on proprietary VLMs. The exact generated reasoning datasets, quality filters, and cost/availability are important for reproducing the claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: improving visual grounding accuracy and latency for deployable small VLMs, with experiments across two model families and several model sizes.

The empirical gains on RefCOCO-style benchmarks are substantial for the reported small models, especially for Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B, and the paper provides useful per-split results rather than only aggregate numbers.

The amodal grounding extension is potentially interesting for robotics/autonomous settings, and the paper makes a reasonable first attempt to construct language-query amodal grounding data from existing amodal annotations.
The appendices include many implementation details, prompts, RL hyperparameters, and dataset sizes, which helps clarify the training pipeline.
weaknesses: The central framing as “test-time scaling” is misleading. The method is primarily supervised fine-tuning on GPT-generated rationales followed by RL; increased output length is a consequence of training, not an isolated test-time scaling mechanism. The paper lacks key ablations comparing plain fine-tuning, reasoning-only SFT, RL-only, longer prompting without training, and different reasoning lengths.

The causal claim that small VLMs mainly fail due to text understanding is weakly supported. The failure taxonomy is generated by GPT-4 using the image, prediction, and ground-truth box, with no human validation or controlled tests separating visual perception, localization, and language parsing. This makes the “COMPLEX PROMPT” diagnosis somewhat circular.

The amodal benchmark construction is not sufficiently reliable as an evaluation contribution. Test prompts are generated from ground-truth boxes/images by a proprietary VLM and then verified by a proprietary VLM, which can bake annotation-dependent cues into the task. There is no human quality audit, inter-annotator validation, leakage analysis, or comparison to natural referring expressions.

The experimental evidence is incomplete for the main claims. There are no statistical confidence intervals, limited analysis of failure modes after EGM, no evaluation beyond RefCOCO-style data and the synthetic amodal benchmark, and no clear robustness tests on genuinely out-of-distribution grounding queries.

Efficiency claims need more care. “GPU latency” as latency multiplied by GPU count is unconventional, and the setup does not fully specify GPU counts, batching, memory constraints, decoding lengths, output-token counts per model, or whether larger models use optimized serving. Training and proprietary data-generation costs are excluded despite being central to the method.

Comparisons to proprietary models such as GPT-5 and Gemini appear implausibly poor and are under-specified; prompt formatting, parsing failures, and model-specific grounding protocols could dominate these numbers. These baselines should not carry much evidential weight as presented.

Originality is limited: the core recipe of GPT-generated chain-of-thought/rationale distillation plus GRPO-style RL is standard. The paper’s value depends on careful empirical validation for grounding, but the current evidence does not convincingly rule out simpler explanations such as extra task-specific supervision or benchmark-specific overfitting.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an acceptance-level systems/algorithm paper: the GitHub and website are marked “coming soon,” proprietary VLMs are used heavily in data generation and evaluation, and some model/data details remain ambiguous. There are also presentation issues, including citation mismatches and occasional overclaiming such as reporting “IoU” where the metric is accuracy at IoU > 0.5.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: improving visual grounding efficiency for deployable small VLMs. The framing of test-time token scaling as an alternative to much larger language backbones is compelling for robotics, autonomous systems, and edge deployment.
weaknesses: The core method is somewhat incremental: GPT-generated reasoning traces, SFT, and GRPO-style RL are established ingredients. The novelty is mainly their application and packaging for grounding rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The diagnosis that small VLMs mainly fail due to language/text understanding is plausible but not fully isolated. The failure taxonomy relies on GPT-based categorization of selected failures, and the analysis does not convincingly rule out visual resolution, attention, detection priors, or training-data effects.

The amodal grounding benchmark is useful, but its construction depends heavily on proprietary VLM-generated prompts and proprietary VLM verification. More human validation, ambiguity analysis, and dataset quality statistics would strengthen confidence that the benchmark measures the intended capability.

Ablations are underdeveloped for the strength of the claims. The paper would benefit from clearer SFT-only vs RL results, reasoning-token budget studies, learnability-selection ablations, reward-component ablations, and comparisons against simply fine-tuning small models without explicit reasoning traces.

Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing: the manuscript says code/GitHub are coming soon, uses proprietary VLMs for data generation and analysis, and does not provide enough detail to independently reconstruct the generated data pipeline or assess its cost.

Some reporting is imprecise. The paper repeatedly describes numbers such as 91.4 as IoU, while the evaluation metric is accuracy at IoU > 0.5. Several proprietary-model baselines also appear surprisingly weak, suggesting prompting/evaluation details may materially affect conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving visual grounding accuracy while reducing deployment latency and model size. The core claim, that smaller VLMs with learned concise multimodal reasoning can match or exceed much larger models, is relevant to edge robotics and autonomous systems.

The empirical results are broad and encouraging. EGM improves multiple Qwen3-VL and InternVL-3 model sizes on RefCOCO/+/g, with especially strong gains for smaller models, and the reported 8B Qwen result slightly exceeds the 235B Qwen baseline while being substantially faster.

The paper includes useful ablations for SFT vs. RL and reasoning vs. restricted non-reasoning outputs, plus hard-sample analysis showing that many previously failed cases become solved after training.

The amodal grounding extension is a valuable direction. Curating referring-expression-style prompts for COCO-Amodal/TAO-Amodal and evaluating VLMs on amodal boxes could be a useful benchmark contribution if released and documented carefully.
The paper is generally clear, with concrete examples of failure modes, training data construction, reward design, and qualitative comparisons that make the proposed behavior easy to understand.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The method is largely a combination of proprietary-model-generated rationales, SFT, GRPO-style RL, IoU-based reward, and learnability-based data selection. These are sensible engineering choices, but the algorithmic contribution beyond adapting existing reasoning/RL recipes to grounding is limited.

The central diagnosis that small VLMs fail mainly because of complex prompts is not fully convincing. The failure labels are produced by proprietary models rather than human annotation, categories overlap, and the disagreement is substantial: for example, GT-error ranges from 0.6% to 27.6% across judges. This weakens the causal motivation.

The evidence that “reasoning” is the main source of improvement is mixed. The w/o-reasoning variant still obtains large gains for some Qwen models, suggesting much of the benefit may come from task-specific SFT/RL on RefCOCO-style data rather than from explicit reasoning traces alone. The ablation also appears to change output constraints, which may confound the comparison.

The efficiency claim is meaningful for inference deployment but incomplete. The approach depends on expensive proprietary VLM data generation, large reference models for learnability selection, and multi-stage training on A100s. The paper should more clearly separate deployment-time efficiency from total pipeline cost.

The amodal benchmark construction relies heavily on proprietary VLM prompt generation and verification, with no clear human validation or analysis of prompt ambiguity/noise on the evaluation split. Since the benchmark is newly created by the authors, its reliability is central to the claimed generality.

Some comparisons may not be fully fair or interpretable. EGM models are task-trained on grounding data, while several large/proprietary baselines may not receive comparable task-specific tuning. The paper should clarify which baselines are fine-tuned, which are zero-shot, and whether training data overlaps with prior model pretraining.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the first page lists GitHub/Website/Models fields but no visible URLs in the extracted manuscript, and key components depend on proprietary models named only at a high level. Releasing the curated data, prompts, model checkpoints, and evaluation scripts would be important for acceptance-level confidence.

There are presentation inaccuracies, such as describing the RefCOCO result as “91.4 IoU” when the metric is actually success accuracy at IoU > 0.5. This does not invalidate the results but should be corrected.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: improving visual grounding performance and latency for smaller VLMs, which is relevant to deployment-constrained vision systems.
The empirical coverage is reasonably broad, with experiments across Qwen3-VL and InternVL model families, multiple model sizes, standard RefCOCO splits, and an additional amodal grounding setting.
Reported RefCOCO gains are nontrivial for several small models, and the latency comparison suggests that fine-tuned smaller models can be a useful alternative to very large VLMs for this task.
The paper includes useful ablations for SFT vs. RL and for reasoning-output removal, plus some qualitative examples that make the intended behavior easy to understand.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited. The method is essentially proprietary-model-generated reasoning traces plus SFT, learnability-based hard-sample selection, and GRPO with a standard IoU/success reward. These ingredients are not new enough, in my view, to support the strength of the paper’s claims without much cleaner evidence.

The central claim that gains come from “reasoning” is not convincingly isolated. The no-reasoning ablation still gives most of the gains for Qwen 2B/4B, and the method also changes training data, hard-sample selection, RL objective, and supervision. This makes it hard to conclude that extended reasoning, rather than task-specific fine-tuning or label-conditioned distillation, is the main driver.

The data-generation pipeline is heavily dependent on unspecified proprietary VLMs that see the ground-truth box or annotations. This creates weak reproducibility and makes the reasoning traces closer to post-hoc label-conditioned rationales than evidence of a transferable reasoning mechanism.

The amodal benchmark is problematic as evidence: prompts are generated and verified by a proprietary VLM, apparently using a pipeline similar to the one used for training data. There is no clear human validation, no analysis of prompt quality or bias, and limited comparison to amodal-specific vision methods. This weakens the claim that the paper establishes a meaningful new amodal grounding benchmark.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. Inference latency is reported, but the cost of proprietary data generation, SFT/RL training on multiple models, and rollout generation is not accounted for. The comparison also relies on a random 10% subset without variance or confidence intervals.

Comparisons to proprietary models such as GPT-5 and Gemini appear surprisingly poor and are not sufficiently explained; parsing, prompting, coordinate conventions, or API limitations could dominate these numbers. This makes those comparisons difficult to trust.

The manuscript has several presentation and rigor issues: it reports “IoU” where the metric is actually accuracy at IoU > 0.5, the GitHub/website/model links are blank, the proprietary curation model is not identified, and statistical uncertainty is absent. These issues are not merely cosmetic because they affect reproducibility and interpretation.

Overall, under the default Algorithms/General framing, the paper has useful empirical observations but does not provide a sufficiently convincing, reproducible, or well-controlled scientific case for acceptance at ECCV.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving visual grounding performance of deployable small VLMs rather than relying on very large models. The efficiency framing is compelling, especially the reported 8B model outperforming Qwen3-VL-235B on RefCOCO average accuracy while being substantially faster in measured latency.

The empirical gains are broad and consistent across two model families and multiple sizes. Improvements on RefCOCO are strong for Qwen3-VL models (+3.6 to +6.0 average accuracy) and present for InternVL models as well, and the SFT/RL ablations support the claim that both stages contribute.

The method is technically reasonable and well motivated: generated grounding rationales plus RL with an IoU/success reward is a plausible way to transfer stronger text/relational reasoning into smaller grounding VLMs. The hard-sample analysis also supports the stated motivation that complex referring expressions are a major failure mode.

The amodal grounding extension is a useful and timely contribution. Even though the benchmark construction has caveats, formulating VLM-based amodal grounding and showing consistent gains across model families broadens the paper beyond standard RefCOCO tuning.

The manuscript is generally clear, with useful implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, dataset sizes, and qualitative examples. The appendix improves transparency relative to many VLM fine-tuning papers.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. The recipe combines proprietary-model generated rationales, SFT, and GRPO-style RL with standard IoU/success rewards. This is effective, but the conceptual advance over recent reasoning-distillation/RL pipelines is more application-specific than fundamentally new.

Reproducibility depends heavily on proprietary VLMs for failure analysis, training rationale generation, amodal prompt generation, and verification. The manuscript gives prompts, but not enough detail on the exact proprietary models, sampling settings, costs, filtering reliability, or whether the generated data/model checkpoints will actually be released.

The amodal benchmark is promising but not fully validated. Text prompts and verification are produced by a proprietary VLM, about 50% of samples are filtered, and there is no human validation of prompt uniqueness or annotation quality. This raises possible selection bias and makes the strength of the amodal conclusions less certain.

The failure-mode analysis that motivates the paper is somewhat weak scientifically: the sample size is not clearly reported in the main text, category assignment is done by proprietary models, and the models disagree substantially, e.g. GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro assign many failures to GT errors or other categories. This supports the intuition but does not conclusively prove that language understanding is the dominant bottleneck.

Some claims and terminology are imprecise. The paper sometimes says “91.4 IoU” when the tables define the metric as accuracy/success rate at IoU > 0.5. The latency comparison would also benefit from fuller reporting of token counts, batch size, hardware utilization, memory footprint, and whether all baselines were equally optimized.

The use of ground-truth boxes highlighted in prompts for rationale generation may create rationales that are partly post-hoc explanations rather than naturally discovered reasoning. This is acceptable for supervised training, but it weakens claims that the model has learned general reasoning rather than box-conditioned explanation patterns unless supported by more out-of-distribution tests.
